props.title: Killing Zoe
props.initialSlug: American's Paris heist spirals into bloody chaos

sections.content: Killing Zoe emerged as a vital entry in the post-Tarantino crime wave, written and directed by Roger Avary (Tarantino's co-writer on Pulp Fiction (1994)). The film follows American safecracker Zed through a hellish 24 hours in Paris, combining the stylized violence of Reservoir Dogs (1992) with a distinctly European art-house sensibility. Avary's direction captures the sweaty, drug-fueled desperation of a heist gone wrong, while Eric Stoltz and Jean-Hugues Anglade deliver raw performances that exemplify the era's indie crime aesthetic. Killing Zoe|1993|An American safecracker gets caught up in a brutal Paris bank heist with his unstable French friend|Prime Video True Romance|1993|A Tarantino-penned crime romance following lovers on the run with stolen cocaine|HBO Max Bad Lieutenant|1992|Harvey Keitel stars as a corrupt cop spiraling into drug addiction and violence|Criterion

The film sits perfectly within the 1990s independent crime thriller movement, alongside works like The Last Seduction (1994) and Red Rock West (1993). What sets Killing Zoe apart is its distinctly French influences, drawing from directors like Jean-Pierre Melville (Le Samouraï (1967)) while maintaining American indie grittiness. The film's bank heist sequence predates similar tensions found in Heat (1995), though Avary opts for claustrophobic chaos over Mann's clinical precision.

The AIDS crisis subtext running through Killing Zoe reflects similar themes in contemporary films like Kids (1995) and Safe (1995). Avary uses the bank robbery genre to explore broader anxieties about contamination, addiction, and American-European relations in the early post-Cold War period. The film's hallucinatory party sequence owes a debt to Trainspotting (1996), though Killing Zoe preceded it by several years. Point Break|1991|FBI agent infiltrates a gang of surfing bank robbers|Netflix City of Industry|1997|Hard-boiled LA heist thriller with Harvey Keitel|Tubi Romeo Is Bleeding|1993|Corrupt cop thriller with Gary Oldman|Prime Video SUBHEAD: The French Connection

Killing Zoe's Paris setting allows it to bridge American and French crime film traditions. While it shares DNA with American indies like One False Move (1992), it also connects to French extremity films that would follow, like High Tension (2003) and Inside (2007). The violence, while shocking for 1993, established a template for the boundary-pushing international co-productions that dominated late 90s genre cinema.
